design_detail: Consensus statement of a panel convened and funded by the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA, Center for Substance Abuse Treatment), published in the Journal of Addictive Diseases (issue July 2013, online 27 September 2013). Who wrote it: 2 co-chairs (a forensic toxicologist, University of Florida; an epidemiologist, University of Texas at Austin), 10 members (forensic toxicologists, two of them heading commercial toxicology laboratories; three medical examiners or forensic pathologists; a past president of the International Association of Coroners and Medical Examiners; an emergency physician and medical toxicologist; a state drug epidemiologist) and 13 ex officio members (Food and Drug Administration 4, Drug Enforcement Administration 2, SAMHSA 3, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention including the National Center for Health Statistics 2, National Institute on Drug Abuse 1, and the project director at the contractor JBS International, who is the corresponding author) (Appendix A). On what evidence: a MEDLINE and Embase search, 1970 to 2012, English language, plus US, Canadian and UK official guidelines and government reports; the panel wrote a preliminary report that was circulated to unnamed experts for review (Methods). No search terms, yield, selection criteria or consensus procedure are reported, recommendations are not graded, and the statement cites 19 references (8 journal articles; 11 reports, manuals, handbooks, guidelines or classifications). Content: recommendations in four areas (scene investigation; toxicological testing, with a nine-point standard; case definitions of drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected deaths and of 'drug', each mapped to vital-statistics categories; determination and documentation of causality on the death certificate), four constructed cases, and a glossary (Appendix B). Filed as narrative-review with the editors' checklist, as the round brief directs for consensus papers. No data.
can_establish: What a SAMHSA-convened US panel of forensic toxicologists, medical examiners and federal agency staff recommended in 2013 as standard definitions for drug-related deaths (drug-caused, drug-poisoning, drug-detected), how it mapped them onto ICD-10 vital-statistics categories, how it advised medical examiners and coroners to test, judge causality and word death certificates, and which sources of error in drug-death counts it names.
cannot_establish: How often deaths are wrongly attributed to, or missed for, any drug, or whether the standards make counts more accurate or more consistent: the statement reports no data, does not describe what its literature search found or how consensus was reached, grades none of its recommendations, and its four cases are constructed examples.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (consensus statement). SAMHSA convened a panel of medical examiners, coroners, toxicologists, epidemiologists and other public health officials to examine the research literature and current practice (Introduction, 3rd paragraph). The impetus came from SAMHSA expert meetings in 2003, 2007 and 2010, which concluded that medical examiners and coroners did not use common definitions for deaths caused by opioids (Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; the cited reports, refs 1, 3 and 4, are SAMHSA reports on methadone-associated mortality).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MEDLINE and Embase, 1970 through 2012, for research articles and clinical guidelines on death classification and case definitions; English-language articles; official guidelines from the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom; relevant government reports (Methods). No search terms, counts or inclusion criteria are given.
sample.selection_effects: US-only panel weighted towards forensic toxicology, medical examiner offices and regulatory agencies (FDA, DEA). No member is listed from drug treatment services or from organisations of people who use drugs, and death-certificate coding is represented only by one NCHS epidemiologist (ex officio), although the Introduction says panel members had backgrounds in addiction medicine, opioid pharmacology, methadone maintenance treatment and medical education (Introduction, 3rd paragraph). The motivating concern was methadone-associated mortality, and the Conclusions frame the definitions around separating deaths caused by methadone from deaths in which it was contributing or merely present.

exposure.measurement: Not a study. The statement's recommendations on establishing drug involvement: a full scene investigation with photographs, collection of drug evidence and a history from family or bystanders; prescription-monitoring records for deaths involving controlled prescription drugs (prescription history, use without a prescription, tolerance); contact with local opioid treatment programmes in methadone or buprenorphine cases (Scene Investigation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs); a nine-point toxicology standard (Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, 6th paragraph and numbered standards 1 to 9); and certification from a synthesis of circumstances, medical and substance-use history, drug source and autopsy findings rather than laboratory values alone (Determination and Documentation of Causality, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable; no amounts are given. The statement recommends that investigators inventory drugs found at the scene, and that the route be recorded, where known, in the 'how injury occurred' field of the certificate (Scene Investigation, 1st paragraph; Determination and Documentation of Causality, 16th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: All drugs judged physiologically significant should be listed individually in Part I of the certificate, by their role in the death rather than their lethality; drugs that did not contribute should not be recorded (they still count as drug-detected); each drug in a mixed intoxication is to be judged alone and in combination, by similarity of mechanism and known additive or synergistic effects; 'multidrug intoxication' and 'polypharmacy' are discouraged; attention is drawn to opioids combined with benzodiazepines, other opioids and alcohol (Determination and Documentation of Causality, 4th, 5th, 7th and 8th paragraphs; Appendix B, Drug Poisoning). The definition of 'drug' excludes alcohol and tobacco, while the toxicology standard includes testing for alcohol.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable. The 'outcomes' are definitions and their stated vital-statistics equivalents: drug-caused death parallels the NCHS category of drug-induced deaths (ICD-10 underlying-cause codes listed in NCHS's annual 'Deaths: Final Data'); drug-poisoning death parallels the drug subset of poisoning, underlying cause X40 to X44 (unintentional), X60 to X64 (suicide), X85 (assault) and Y10 to Y14 (undetermined intent); 'drug' corresponds roughly to T36 to T50; drug-detected death maps to no ICD-10 codes (Case Definitions).
outcomes.validity_norms: The definitions were not tested in this paper for agreement between certifiers or for their effect on counts.
outcomes.operationalization: Drug-caused death: certified as resulting from exposure to a drug, alone or with other substances, whatever the intent; includes acute toxicity, chronic drug effects, adverse reactions, legal executions, terrorist events and mental and behavioural disorders due to drugs; excludes infections resulting from drug use (for example from injecting) and congenital anomalies. Drug-poisoning death (proposed subcategory): certified as due to acute exposure, the lay concept of an overdose, whatever the intent; excludes chronic effects, adverse effects of a correct drug properly given, executions, terrorism and mental and behavioural disorders. Drug-detected death: a drug found on post-mortem testing whatever its role, including natural and trauma deaths; excludes deaths in which toxicology was done before death in hospital. For the first two, toxicology is usually but not always required: in rare cases circumstantial evidence may suffice when testing was unavailable or omitted (Case Definitions).

analysis.effect_sizes: None: the statement contains no data.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol and no consensus method (voting, Delphi or other) is described; the external reviewers of the preliminary report are not named and their input is not summarised.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable in the usual sense. What the literature search found, and which sources support which recommendation, is not reported; Case 4 omits the drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected classification lines given for Cases 1 to 3.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A set of definitions, laboratory and certification recommendations and four constructed cases, agreed by a SAMHSA-convened panel and reviewed by unnamed experts, with no data on how drug deaths were being classified or on how much the standards would change the counts.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say that “Concise, scientifically accurately, universally accepted” case definitions like those presented can address a critical distinction (Conclusions); read as describing the panel's own definitions, no evidence of acceptance is offered for definitions the statement itself proposes, though the sentence can also be read as what such definitions could do once adopted. They say the definitions address the distinction between deaths caused by methadone and deaths in which methadone is a contributing factor or merely present, but the definitions fold contributing drugs into 'drug-caused' and separate only caused from detected, and they apply to all drugs, not methadone. The claim that adoption will improve the quality of data is untested. Case 1 presents a determination of death by multidrug intoxication as highly compelling when the concentrations are described as low-toxic, resting on the history, an assumed tolerance and metabolism during a coma of unknown length (Determination and Documentation of Causality, 13th to 15th paragraphs); this shows that, under the panel's approach, attribution can rest on circumstances rather than on the measured levels, a point the statement does not discuss as a source of over-attribution. The Introduction's description of panel members' backgrounds (addiction medicine, methadone maintenance treatment) does not match the Appendix A list.

timeline.event: National Association of Medical Examiners position paper on certifying cocaine-related deaths (Stephens et al., 2004; ref 19), cited for listing only the contributing drug.
Review of methodological complexities in counting opioid overdose deaths, with Goldberger among its authors (card sc_slavova_2019, this reader).

National Association of Medical Examiners position paper on investigating, diagnosing and certifying deaths related to opioids and other drugs (read by another reader in this round; an earlier opioid-only version is dated 2014 in the project's list).

replication.where_it_stands: A consensus document, not a study, so replication does not apply. The project's reading list names it with Beynon et al. (2007) as the only peer-reviewed comparisons of definitions its PubMed search found (search-logs/DrugDeaths_DOI-LIST.md, section 1, Known gaps). Whether its definitions were adopted, and whether they changed counts, has to be shown by later studies (for example the medical examiners' position paper and studies of certification practice on the same list); this statement cannot show it.

funding.funder: Funding support from the Center for Substance Abuse Treatment of the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, US Department of Health and Human Services. The paper states that SAMHSA had no role in data collection, analysis or manuscript preparation, and that all panel members had access to the data, took part in its interpretation and approved the manuscript; the views are those of the panel and not necessarily of SAMHSA or the Department (author notes).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest or competing-interests statement is printed.
funding.affiliations_note: SAMHSA convened and charged the panel; a SAMHSA medical officer (Center for Substance Abuse Treatment) served as Government Project Officer and is the third author, and three SAMHSA staff were ex officio members, which sits awkwardly beside the statement that SAMHSA had no role in manuscript preparation. The corresponding author is the project director at the contractor (JBS International). Two panel members headed commercial toxicology laboratories (Drugscan, Inc.; NMS Labs), whose services a comprehensive testing standard would extend; ex officio members came from FDA and DEA. Flags for closer reading, not reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Give the same set of complete death-investigation files to several medical examiners and coroners and measure their agreement on drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected categories and on the drugs named, before and after training in these standards; and compare drug-death counts in jurisdictions that adopted the standards with those that did not, against an independent enhanced review of each death.

domains.note: Databases and years are named, but there are no search terms, yield, selection criteria or link from the evidence to each recommendation; 11 of the 19 references are reports, manuals, handbooks, guidelines or classifications.
No source is appraised and no recommendation is graded; the toxicology standard and the causality rules are given without supporting studies.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The case for standardisation rests on SAMHSA's own earlier meetings (refs 1, 3, 4); a co-chair's paper (ref 5) and a panel member's book (ref 14) are cited; otherwise the evidence is the panel's own expertise.

Recommendations are labelled as the panel's, but none says whether it rests on evidence or on judgment; Case 1 presents a circumstantial determination with low-toxic concentrations as highly compelling; the Conclusions' sentence on 'universally accepted' definitions like those presented can be read as claiming acceptance for the panel's own.

domains.domain: Balance of panel membership and of attention to over- and under-attribution of deaths to drugs
domains.note: The statement names undercounting (immunoassay gaps, no standard thresholds, non-specific certificate wording, morphine and heroin confused) and overcounting (incidental findings, detected against caused, unreported sampling site), but gives no guidance on recording uncertainty, and its worked cases favour attribution in the ambiguous case. Treatment services and people who use drugs are not represented, despite the Introduction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a consensus statement; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, as the round brief directs, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domains (search and appraisal, both high). The statement can be cited, attributed to the SAMHSA consensus panel, for its definitions of drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected deaths and of 'drug', for the ICD-10 equivalents it gives, for its recommendations on toxicology, certificate wording and listing every contributing drug, for the coding consequence of wording (acute intoxication terms coded as poisoning, X42 with T40.5 for cocaine, against 'use' or 'abuse' coded to F14), and for the sources of error it names in both directions. It cannot be cited for any quantity (how often deaths are misattributed or missed), for the adoption or effect of its standards, or for its toxicology claims as established findings, since none is supported by cited studies in the text.

key_findings.finding: SAMHSA convened the panel after expert meetings in 2003, 2007 and 2010 concluded that medical examiners and coroners did not appear to use common definitions for deaths caused by opioids, and that their definitions might differ from those used on death certificates; the panel's charge was to separate deaths caused by a drug from deaths in which the drug was detected but was not a major cause of or contributor to death.

Evidence base and process: MEDLINE and Embase, 1970 through 2012, English-language research articles and clinical guidelines, plus US, Canadian and UK official guidelines and government reports; the panel wrote a preliminary report that was circulated to experts for review, and their input was incorporated. Panel: 2 co-chairs, 10 members and 13 ex officio members from FDA, DEA, SAMHSA, CDC/NCHS, NIDA and the contractor.

Sources of undercounting named in toxicology: immunoassays vary in what they detect, and many do not detect oxycodone and hydromorphone; laboratories use no standard detection threshold; the panel says the lack of standard practice may lead to underreporting of prescription opioids in the deceased. Standards of routine toxicology vary across death-investigation systems; the commonest approach is an immunoassay screen of urine with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry confirmation.
key_findings.locator: Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Measured concentrations vary with the sampling site, route, chronicity of use, time from use to sampling and from death to sampling, and collection method; peripheral (iliac or femoral) blood is the most reliable, yet the site is often not reported, and heart blood, subclavian blood, body-cavity fluid, spleen squeeze or embalming-contaminated blood may all be reported simply as 'blood', which the panel calls an avoidable source of error.

Nine-point standard of forensic toxicology practice: record the sampling site and use peripheral vessels where possible; collect and test admission blood and urine, as opposed to autopsy specimens, where applicable and available; test comprehensively for prescription, illicit and over-the-counter drugs and alcohol; emphasise urine for detection; use an immunoassay screen of defined sensitivity with supplementary assays for drugs with poor cross-reactivity; measure free and total drug in blood, ideally with glucuronide metabolites; test other tissues where blood may be compromised by post-mortem artefact; use similar cut-offs for confirmatory GC-MS and LC-MS; use validated, controlled methods.
key_findings.locator: Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, 6th paragraph and numbered standards 1 to 9

key_findings.finding: Drug-caused death: a death certified as resulting from exposure to a drug, alone or with other substances, whatever the intent (unintentional, suicide, homicide, undetermined); includes acute toxicity, chronic drug effects, adverse drug reactions, legal executions, terrorist events and mental and behavioural disorders due to drugs; excludes infections resulting from drug use and congenital anomalies. It parallels the NCHS category of drug-induced deaths, which also includes adverse effects of drugs in therapeutic use.
key_findings.locator: Case Definitions › 1. Drug-Caused Death, Concept, Includes, Excludes and Equivalent Category

key_findings.finding: Drug-poisoning death (proposed subcategory): a death certified as due to acute exposure to a drug, meant to match the lay concept of an overdose, whatever the intent; includes acute toxicity from recreational use, drugs given or taken in error, drugs prescribed to another person and overdose in a medical setting; excludes infections, congenital anomalies, chronic effects, adverse effects of a correct drug properly given, executions, terrorism and mental and behavioural disorders. Equivalent: an ICD-10 underlying cause of X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85 or Y10 to Y14.

Drug-detected death: a drug found on post-mortem testing whatever its role, including natural and trauma deaths (for example motor vehicle crashes, suffocation) and all drug-caused and drug-poisoning deaths; excludes deaths whose toxicology was done before death by hospital staff; maps to no ICD-10 codes. The panel notes it is simpler for medical examiners and coroners to report because it can be drawn from their own laboratory database without cut-points.

'Drug': any compound used for diagnosis, treatment or prevention, for relief of pain, to control a physiological or pathological condition, or for the feeling it causes; includes illicit drugs (heroin, cocaine, hallucinogens), prescription and over-the-counter drugs, biological substances and inhaled solvents; excludes alcohol, tobacco and noxious substances eaten as food, such as hallucinogenic mushrooms; corresponds roughly to ICD-10 T36 to T50.

Causality is to be judged from circumstances, medical and substance-use history, drug source and autopsy, not laboratory values alone, including whether the pre-terminal events fit the drug's action and whether the person was likely tolerant; the panel singles out accumulation of long half-life drugs such as methadone in the first days of treatment, and overdose after tolerance has fallen during a period without the drug (for example in prison or hospital). Competing natural or external causes and mixed intoxications complicate certification.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Certificate rules: list every drug judged physiologically significant individually in Part I, by its role rather than its lethality, and conditions that contributed but did not cause the underlying cause in Part II; list a drug in Part I when the certifier concludes it caused death even without toxicology; leave non-contributing drugs off the certificate; name individual drugs rather than 'drug intoxication' or 'polypharmacy', because certificates are the source of national mortality statistics; record the parent drug, and specify heroin rather than morphine when 6-acetylmorphine or the circumstances point to heroin.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 5th to 9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Wording decides the code: acute cocaine intoxication, acute cocaine toxicity, toxic effects of cocaine, cocaine poisoning and cocaine overdose are all coded as poisoning, X42 with T40.5, whereas cocaine use, cocaine abuse, cocaine snorting and cocaine addiction are coded to F14 (mental and behavioural disorders due to cocaine). The panel advises 'toxicity', 'intoxication' or 'poisoning' for acute deaths, 'use', 'abuse', 'dependence' or 'disorder' only when substance use itself is meant as the cause, and avoiding 'overdose', which lacks a specific meaning.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 10th to 12th paragraphs; Appendix B, Drug Poisoning (Overdose)

key_findings.finding: Case 1: a 40-year-old man with a history of substance use disorder who used drugs with friends, went to sleep and could not be woken the next day, with pulmonary congestion and oedema at autopsy and toxicology showing low-toxic concentrations of oxycodone and diazepam, is certified as acute intoxication by oxycodone and diazepam (drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected). The panel reasons that he was expected to be opioid-tolerant and would have metabolised much of the drug during the coma, so the circumstances are highly compelling even though the concentrations are not classically lethal; diazepam is listed because it contributed to respiratory depression.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 13th to 16th paragraphs (Case 1)
key_findings.note: The attribution rests on circumstances and assumed tolerance and metabolism, not on the measured concentrations; the comment also invokes ethanol, which the case does not report finding.

key_findings.finding: Case 2: a 45-year-old woman treated for years with opioid analgesics for fibromyalgia, prescribed methadone 4 days earlier, with a methadone concentration toxic to a non-tolerant person and no other findings, is certified as acute intoxication by methadone with chronic pain in Part II, and described as not tolerant to the drug's effects.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 17th and 18th paragraphs (Case 2)

key_findings.finding: Case 3: a 22-year-old man shot in the head while selling cocaine, with a lethal concentration of a drug on toxicology, is certified as death from gunshot wounds: not drug-caused and not drug-poisoning, but drug-detected; the panel keeps the drug off the cause-of-death statement and says drug-detected counts still matter for statistics on illicit drug use.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 19th to 21st paragraphs (Case 3)

key_findings.finding: Case 4: a 52-year-old man with hypertension who collapsed after smoking crack cocaine, with a hypertensive-type intracerebral haemorrhage and alcohol and alprazolam also found, is certified as intracerebral haemorrhage due to acute cocaine toxicity, with hypertension in Part II and an accidental manner (the non-natural manner preferred when intoxication exacerbates natural disease); only cocaine is listed, as alprazolam likely did not contribute.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 22nd and 23rd paragraphs (Case 4)

key_findings.finding: Who decides: medical examiners are described as appointed, professionally trained forensic pathologists who certify cause and manner of death; coroners as elected or appointed officials with widely varying qualifications who, if not physicians, must use coroners' physicians for autopsies. Manner options on the US certificate: natural, accidental, homicide, suicide, pending investigation, could not be determined.
key_findings.locator: Appendix B › Medical Examiner and Coroner; Appendix B › Death Certification

key_findings.finding: Scene investigation: inspect the whole scene, photograph it, collect all evidence of possible exposure to drugs, take a history from family members or bystanders, and inventory the drugs to determine or estimate the amount taken; in deaths involving controlled prescription drugs, request the person's records from the state prescription drug monitoring programme, where one exists, for prescription history and evidence of use without a prescription, which the panel says help to judge tolerance, and to find the health care providers who hold the medical history; in methadone or buprenorphine deaths, contact local opioid treatment programmes to learn whether the person received the drug from them, where the jurisdiction allows it.
key_findings.locator: Discussion and Recommendations › Scene Investigation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The panel asks that toxicology measurements also be judged on whether they can distinguish acute from chronic drug use, for example by measuring free and glucuronidated metabolites, which current bench-top liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry makes more feasible, and says that collecting such data on drug-related deaths may give indicators for judging future cases.
key_findings.note: No reference is cited in that paragraph.

reporting_issues.issue: The drug-detected definition contradicts itself: its laboratory criterion says evidence of the drug must be found on post-mortem toxicology, then allows the definition to be met on circumstantial evidence when testing was unavailable; it says it includes all drug-caused and drug-poisoning deaths, yet excludes deaths whose only toxicology was done in hospital before death. Its circumstantial-evidence sentence even ends by speaking of certifying the death as a drug poisoning death, apparently carried over from definition 1-a.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Case Definitions › 2. Drug-Detected Death, Laboratory Criteria, Includes and Excludes
reporting_issues.consequence: A drug-caused death certified without post-mortem toxicology, or after hospital testing only, is in one category and out of the other, so drug-detected counts are not a superset of drug-caused counts as stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The definition of 'drug' includes hallucinogens among illicit drugs but excludes hallucinogenic mushrooms as noxious substances eaten as food, and excludes alcohol, while the toxicology standard tests for alcohol and the Case 1 comment refers to ethanol although none is reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Case Definitions › 3. Drug; Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, standard 3; Case 1 comment
reporting_issues.consequence: Under these definitions deaths involving psilocybin-containing mushrooms or alcohol alone would not count as drug deaths; claims should state the definitions' boundaries rather than treat 'drug death' as self-evident.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction says panel members had backgrounds in addiction medicine, opioid pharmacology, methadone maintenance treatment and medical education, but the Appendix A list shows forensic toxicologists, medical examiners, a coroners' association past president, a medical toxicologist, epidemiologists and agency staff, none described as working in addiction treatment. The nearest are two ex officio members from SAMHSA's Division of Pharmacologic Therapies (Center for Substance Abuse Treatment), listed with federal agency titles; the Introduction also says the panel included representatives of organisations committed to the safety and effectiveness of opioid addiction treatment.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Appendix A
reporting_issues.consequence: The panel's composition should be described from Appendix A, not from the Introduction.

reporting_issues.issue: The funding note says SAMHSA had no role in data collection, analysis or manuscript preparation, although SAMHSA convened and charged the panel, a SAMHSA medical officer served as Government Project Officer and is an author, and three SAMHSA staff were ex officio members; no competing-interests statement is printed for any panel member. The same note says all panel members had access to the data, although the statement reports none.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, author notes; Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Appendix A
reporting_issues.consequence: The agency's role should be described as convening, funding and co-authoring; interests of members from commercial laboratories and regulators are undeclared.

reporting_issues.issue: Case 2 calls a woman treated for years with various opioid analgesics not tolerant to the drug's effects (methadone, started 4 days earlier) without saying why that history gave no tolerance; the induction-period risk described in the 2nd paragraph of the causality section (long half-life drugs such as methadone accumulating in the first days of treatment, before tolerance develops) fits the case but is left implicit. Case 1 infers tolerance from a history of substance use disorder and uses assumed tolerance and metabolism during a coma to support attribution despite low-toxic concentrations.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Determination and Documentation of Causality, 2nd and 13th to 18th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Tolerance is inferred from history, not measured: assumed present in Case 1 and absent in Case 2, and in both the inference supports attribution; the cases illustrate the panel's reasoning, not a tested rule.

reporting_issues.issue: Case 4 omits the drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected classification lines given for Cases 1 to 3, although it is the case that most tests the definitions (a drug precipitating death from natural disease); it also says toxicology indicated acute cocaine intoxication, a judgment the statement elsewhere says laboratory values alone cannot make.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Determination and Documentation of Causality, 22nd and 23rd paragraphs; 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: How the panel would count a cocaine-precipitated haemorrhage under its own categories is left to inference.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions describe a three-way distinction between deaths caused by methadone and deaths in which it is contributing or merely present, but the definitions provide two (drug-caused, which includes contributing drugs, and drug-detected) and cover all drugs.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the definitions themselves, not the summary in the Conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: Typographical errors: 'SAMSHA' (Introduction, 1st paragraph), 'a certain opioids' (Abstract), 'listed as a the cause of death', 'Terms such as such as', 'scientifically accurately', 'Coroners Medical Examiners', 'causes about death' and 'did not contribute the death' (Case 4 comment); the panel is called the Consensus Panel and the Expert Panel interchangeably.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Introduction; Case Definitions › 2; Determination and Documentation of Causality; Conclusions

reporting_issues.issue: Standard 2 of the toxicology standard asks for admission blood and urine to be collected and tested, as opposed to autopsy specimens, where applicable and available, while the drug-detected definition requires evidence of the drug on post-mortem toxicology and excludes deaths whose toxicology was performed before death by hospital staff; the statement does not say whether a drug found only in admission specimens, tested after death by the medical examiner's laboratory, makes a death drug-detected.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, numbered standard 2; Case Definitions › 2. Drug-Detected Death, Laboratory Criteria and Excludes
reporting_issues.consequence: How such deaths are counted is left to each office, so drug-detected counts can differ with laboratory practice as well as with the deaths themselves.
